job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Diego Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Diego. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I'm at Sandford University doing a master's in industrial automation and controls. I rent a room in student housing, six of us sharing a kitchen. Friday evening I take the bus home, and Saturdays I ride in my dad's van, the one that says Lopez Electrical on the side. We do rewires, fuse boxes and the odd shop fit-out, and I hold the ladder and read the drawings. Sundays are my grandmother's lunch and a football match on the park.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electronic engineering, a pass. My final project was a controller for a greenhouse irrigation system, and it worked, but my write-up was rushed because I was covering Dad's jobs when his back went. No internship. Dad's business barely pays him a wage, so there's no money to spare. I owe about twenty-eight thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I thought: some noise, a few useful tools, and then life goes on. I'd tell my dad's customers that a robot isn't going to crawl through their loft. I'd be relaxed saying it, because the trade I grew up in isn't about screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes: I'm still a graduate with a pass, no internship and debt. There aren't many firms around here that hire engineers, and they want master's and experience. I could always work for Dad, but the van doesn't pay two wages. So my worry is about the money in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and look at jobs in industrial controls, which suits what I've studied: factories, water plants, anything with a panel. I'd also keep working Saturdays with Dad, and I'd talk to him about taking a certified course so the business can bid for bigger jobs. I use AI tools sometimes to check my wiring calculations, and I'd continue. I'd save 80 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, but okay. I'm used to being short of money, so it doesn't feel like a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the van doesn't pay two wages. How does the business actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad earns about as much as a teacher. Last year two of his steady customers, a letting agency and a small builder, cut their orders. He does the invoices at the kitchen table at night. I try to help but he doesn't like me seeing the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The football on Sundays, if I can't afford the bus fare. After that, my phone contract. I'd never cut the Saturday work with Dad. I don't do the Saturday work for the pay, I do it because Dad would otherwise be up the ladder alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a real change, but that it'll hit desks before it hits ladders. People who work with their hands and take pride in doing it right will be okay for a good while. I'd say that to my friends who sit at laptops all day, and I'd mean it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd say the design and planning jobs that a graduate like me would normally start in are the ones getting squeezed. But the hands-on side of electrical and controls work, installing and fixing, stays needed for longer. So I'd have two doors: the graduate job and Dad's trade. Neither door is wide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for jobs that mix the two: commissioning engineer, controls technician, maintenance at a plant. I'd also get my electrician's certification so I can sign off work, which opens up both Dad's business and others. I'd learn the AI tools once a few more people I trust have shown they work, and then I'd use them for quotes and paperwork. I'd keep the Saturdays with Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit anxious about money, but proud that my family trade looks sturdy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the certification change for Dad's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets us take bigger jobs, like office fit-outs, that need a certified person. Right now Dad does it all himself and he's 56. With two of us qualified, we could take three jobs a month instead of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who lost a desk job to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come and spend a Saturday on the van, and I'd mean it. It's not a glamorous job, but it's honest work, and it pays. I'd also say there's no shame in changing, because my dad did it at 30.

I'd say it kindly to friends at laptops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a joke. I'd say that families, firms and the government won't be ready, and that I'd want the people at the top to say honestly what they plan. I'd also say we should look after each other, because that's what neighbours do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's frightening. I finish the master's in a year and walk into a market where the engineering side is done by AI. Robots for hands-on jobs take until 2031, so Dad's trade would hold up a while, but a van with two wages and then a robot arm is a different future. I'd have debt, nothing saved and a family business that may fold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the master's if a controls job came up, and otherwise finish it and go straight into the van. I'd get the electrician's certification quickly and push Dad to bid for jobs that robots won't do soon: older buildings, repairs. I'd cut every cost, move back home, and cook for the family. I'd also talk to my grandmother's church group about help for families like ours. And I'd vote for anyone serious about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like I'm walking toward a river with no bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a family business that may fold. What would happen then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would be 58 with no pension to speak of and a bad back. I'd be the main earner, on a graduate salary I haven't got. My mother cleans two houses, and that would carry us for a while. That's the picture that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fact that robots for physical jobs take three more years. If I'm ready by 2028 for repair and installation work, I'd have until 2031 to build something solid. It's not much, but it's more than a desk job has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to adapt if you start, and I'd say so. I'd say the answer isn't handouts, it's training and a fair chance to work, and that employers should keep taking apprentices. I'd say it to my dad's customers and anyone else who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious but I think I'd manage. I'd have a few years of work in controls or with Dad before the thinking side is taken, and then until about 2034 on the hands-on side. That's long enough to get qualified and save. I'd still worry about Dad's business, because he's slow to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take an industrial controls job, and keep the Saturdays. I'd get the electrician's certification and start learning how to install and maintain small automation, because those are the jobs that need a person with a screwdriver. I'd save 150 a month and clear the loan with the highest rate. And I'd help Dad try one AI tool for quotes, to see if it saves him evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit steadier. I'd feel like a man with a plan, even if the plan is full of unknowns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dad is slow to change. How would you handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly, and with respect. I'd show him one thing at a time, like how a quote could be drafted in two minutes. If he sees it save him an evening, he'll use it, because he doesn't waste time. I'd never tell him he's doing it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting an engineering degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take every internship, even unpaid, because I didn't and I paid for it. Learn the tools, but also learn something with your hands. A degree can be copied by a machine, but a person who can fix the fuse box on a Sunday is hard to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is time, and I'd say that's good news for people who start. I'd say we should train young people in trades and technology together, and give small businesses help to adapt. I'd say it with a smile, because I'm a bit of an optimist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but fine. I'd be 34 in 2036, with a trade, a degree and maybe a small business with my father. The debt would be gone, and I might be married. The worry is that Dad's business doesn't survive the middle years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a controls job, get certified and save for a deposit. Over the years I'd build Lopez Electrical into something that does installation and automation maintenance, and take on an apprentice. I'd adopt the tools once they're proven, which is how I've always done it. I'd also look after Dad and my grandmother, because family is the point of all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. I'd say content, but I'm cautious about saying that word out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the business look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two vans and an apprentice, maybe an office with a small sign. We'd do fuse boxes and rewires as now, plus maintenance contracts for small factories' control panels. Dad would still turn up on Saturdays and complain about my wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most along the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd wait too long to try something new. I like to see things proven before I use them, and a decade is a long time to sit on a wall. I'd put a review in my diary every year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It hits Dad's income and mine at the same time, and there'd be no space to retrain or save. What would help is a proper apprenticeship system, support for small family firms to adapt, and honest information from the government about what's coming. I'd also like a way to get a first job without having done an unpaid internship.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say we shouldn't forget the people who keep the lights on. A lot of talk about AI is about desks, and I come from a family that works with ladders. I think they'd cope better than most, but only if someone helps small firms keep up.

headlineQuote: A lot of talk about AI is about desks, and I come from a family that works with ladders.
portrait: Diego is 24, doing a master's in **industrial automation**, and rides in his dad's electrician's van on Saturdays.
He passed his electronic engineering degree with **no internship** and owes about twenty-eight thousand.
His father's small business, **Lopez Electrical**, barely pays one wage, so there is no money to spare.
He's traditional and steady: work over handouts, family first, and new tools once they are **proven**.
His moods run from anxious to alarmed, and he is hopeful when he can picture the family business **growing**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most: it hits his dad's income and his own at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **apprenticeship** system and support for small family firms to adapt.
